doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Working with Cannonball and the end of Riverside
summary: He describes Cannonball's 1958-64 tenure, Cannonball's offer to extend his contract, and having to refuse as Riverside collapsed.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Oh they had a very strong sense of arrangements, strong sense of composition in that band. The best way to describe my feelings about Julian Adderley is that I have learned over the years that no matter how close you can become to someone when you are working together, it is extremely difficult to maintain that relationship after the end of the © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

period of working together. Because the circumstances change. I mean you don’t have that regularity because practically you’re always either planning or doing or coming off of a record date when you’re working together. And there’s a great deal of planning together and hanging out together. And when that goes, what you have to recognize is you’re not going to have in most cases, that same kind of closeness. And you have to realize nobody’s mad at anybody necessarily. Sometimes yes, but very often not, it’s just that your paths don’t cross that often and you’re working paths are now different. So I have over the years become very used to that fact that some people who I was very close to when we were working together, there was a falling off of that. Now I worked with Cannonball for a six year period from 1958 to 1964. The end of that relationship was when Riverside collapsed and had its financial disaster and was no more. Incidentally right up to the end of that period Cannonball, whose contract was expiring at almost exactly what turned out to be the time that the company expired, he was pushing on me. He said look I know how unsettled everything is. I was fighting very hard. My partner had died from a heart attack the previous December. Everything about the company was heavily mortgaged and we were really in hock and struggling to stay alive, had no idea whether we were going to make it or not. Cannonball said to me look, obviously if you can announce that you are retaining your major artist, and Cannon was our major selling artist, that’s going to be helpful to you. So why don’t we just — he says I don’t know any more than you do how long you’re going to last, but why don’t we just announce that you have re-signed me, and what we will do is we will continue the present contract for one more year, under the same terms. And believe me he was worth a hell of a lot more. Just extend it as is for a year, give you that year of breathing room, let’s see what develops. Actually what I finally had to do was to tell him, and we equivocated and went back and forth, him offering, me saying I don’t know, and at one point I remember he was working someplace in Upstate New York and we were on the phone together and I said look Julian, I have made a final decision. Wonderful as you are you’re not going to be enough — nothing is going to be enough to ensure the survival of this company and I don’t want you trapped into an ongoing agreement with a dead company that has passed into somebody else’s hands, so what I am telling you is this is a definite decision. If I call you tomorrow and tell you something else don’t pay attention to that. This is it. Go away. So I literally had to kick my star act out of the house. But an indication of what kind of a guy he was is that he had made that offer. And then the important thing and in light of what I’ve been saying about when you’re not working together, we next got together in 1973, when I first joined Fantasy. I was hired to come out to California to run the expanding Fantasy Records jazz program.
